chapterTitle: LLM Tool Calling and Function Execution

beats.headline: Does the LLM actually run your Java code?
beats.subline: It never touches your JVM. Here is the JSON-schema handshake that makes it possible.
beats.narration: If you think the LLM executes your Java methods directly, you are wrong. It is a pure JSON-schema handshake. The model outputs a tool call, and your Spring service executes the logic.

beats.title: The Tool-Calling Loop
beats.subtitle: Model requests, Java executes
beats.narration: The model emits a tool call payload. Spring AI intercepts this, runs your Java method, and feeds the result back into the conversation history for the final synthesis.

beats.title: Registering Tools

steps.explanation: Registers the method as an LLM-accessible function.
Provides the model with schema hints for arguments.
Injected server-side; NEVER exposed to the model.

beats.narration: Use @Tool and @ToolParam to expose methods. Crucially, ToolContext is injected server-side by Spring, keeping sensitive identity data hidden from the LLM's context window.

beats.title: Identity Security
beats.narration: Never let the model supply the userId. That is an open invitation for prompt injection. Always extract the identity from a secure ToolContext on the server side.

beats.title: Part 1 Done
takeaways: Tool calling is a JSON-schema handshake
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Bounding iterations to prevent infinite loops →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we stop runaway LLM loops with manual execution management.

beats.headline: What if the model gets stuck in a loop?
beats.subline: Unbounded tool calls will burn your tokens and crash your threads.
beats.narration: If an LLM keeps retrying broken arguments, it will burn tokens and stall your request threads. You need a hard iteration cap in production.

beats.title: Manual Execution Control

steps.explanation: Disable auto-execution to take control of the loop.
Hard limit prevents runaway token usage.

beats.narration: Set internal tool execution to false. Now, you drive the loop with a ToolCallingManager, allowing you to enforce a strict iteration cap and audit every single step.

beats.title: Audit Logging
beats.caption: Trace every tool decision
beats.narration: Structured logging is mandatory. Log the tool name, the principal, and the iteration count. If it hits your limit, kill the request and audit the failure.

beats.title: Auto vs Manual
beats.narration: Auto-execution is fine for quick prototypes. But for enterprise services, you need the deterministic control of manual execution.

beats.title: Part 2 Done
takeaways: Always enforce a max iteration cap
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: The hidden danger of indirect prompt injection →
beats.narration: Now your loops are safe. In Part 3, we tackle the silent killer: indirect prompt injection.

beats.headline: Is your LLM reading a Trojan horse?
beats.subline: Indirect prompt injection hides commands in PDFs and emails.
beats.narration: An LLM cannot distinguish between user data and instructions. If it reads an email containing a hidden override command, it will execute it. This is indirect prompt injection.

beats.title: The Injection Vector
beats.subtitle: Data is not code
beats.narration: The model reads a document, hits a hidden command, and triggers a tool call. Because the model is already authenticated, your backend treats the malicious call as legitimate.

beats.title: Hardened Validation

steps.explanation: Enforce strict schema constraints on all inputs.
Verify identity against the record, not the LLM.

beats.narration: Validate every input using Jakarta Bean Validation. Then, re-verify ownership against the database. Never assume the LLM's arguments are safe.

beats.title: Tool Privileges
beats.narration: Apply the principle of least privilege. Only register read-only tools when processing untrusted content. Never mix write-capable tools with external data ingestion.

beats.title: Part 3 Done
takeaways: Data is not code: treat all inputs as untrusted
Validate arguments with Jakarta Bean Validation
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Human-in-the-loop for high-risk actions →
beats.narration: Security is a process, not a toggle. In Part 4, we gate high-risk mutations behind human approval.

beats.headline: Never let an LLM move money alone.
beats.subline: High-risk mutations require a cryptographic human gate.
beats.narration: For high-risk actions like refunds or transfers, do not execute the mutation inside the tool. Use a pending-approval pattern instead.

beats.title: The Approval Gate
beats.subtitle: Safe mutations
beats.narration: Persist a pending record with a unique token. The LLM returns a status to the user, and the actual mutation only triggers after an out-of-band human confirmation.

beats.title: Implementing HITL

steps.explanation: Create a secure record instead of executing.
Inform the model that human action is required.

beats.narration: If the value is high, create a pending record and return the status. This prevents the LLM from unilaterally executing high-risk business logic.
